Addis Ababa needs a confident African diplomacy that joins national ambition to regional prosperity The author (Archive) By Mohamud A. Ahmed – Cagaweyne The most consequential victory in diplomacy often comes before negotiations begin: the power to decide what the argument is about. Egypt has long understood this. When the Nile dispute is presented principally as a question of Egyptian survival, Ethiopia’s development arrives in the conversation already under suspicion. A dam becomes a threat before it becomes a source of electricity. An upstream population’s aspirations become a problem for downstream officials to assess. Ethiopia is left explaining why its future should be permitted to advance. This is a profoundly unequal starting point. Egypt’s dependence on the Nile is real, and any responsible settlement must protect its people against serious harm. But dependence does not confer ownership. Historical advantage cannot become perpetual jurisdiction over another country’s economic choices. The weakness in Cairo’s approach emerges whenever a legitimate demand for security expands into an expectation of control. Prime Minister Dr. Abiy Ahmed’s recent remarks at the 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa offered a constructive foundation for challenging that imbalance. Speaking in Bahir Dar, he placed dependable maritime access within Ethiopia’s long-term security and developmental interests. “For a nation of more than 130 million people, access to the sea is existential,” he said, according to the Ethiopian News Agency’s October 24 report. He also affirmed that Ethiopia would pursue its aspirations through dialogue and mutual benefit. That combination deserves support: clarity about the national interest, coupled with a peaceful method for advancing it. The importance of this argument extends beyond ports. It asks whether Ethiopia’s needs will be treated as enduring realities to accommodate or recurring ambitions to contain. Its population needs reliable electricity, competitive industries, dependable trade routes, and the capacity to withstand external disruption. These requirements will survive changes of government. A regional strategy that assumes Ethiopia can indefinitely absorb the costs of inadequate infrastructure and constrained connectivity mistakes postponed development for permanent acquiescence. National security includes the material foundations of ordinary life. A hospital awaiting equipment, a manufacturer facing uncertain delivery costs, and a farmer seeking access to distant markets all depend upon systems that connect Ethiopia to the world. Abiy’s Tana remarks situated maritime access within that larger concern and linked reliable corridors to African trade and economic opportunity. This provides a persuasive direction for diplomacy: Ethiopia can explain how dependable access would benefit coastal partners, producers and communities along transport routes. Egypt’s leadership should recognize the consistency this demands. A country that asks the world to understand its geographical dependence on the Nile should be prepared to understand Ethiopia’s geographical dependence on transit arrangements. The circumstances differ, but the principle is straightforward. Geography creates vulnerabilities that diplomacy must manage fairly. Cairo weakens its moral authority whenever it seeks broad accommodation for Egyptian necessity while approaching Ethiopian necessity chiefly as a strategic inconvenience. The opening of the ninth Cairo Water Week on October 25 demonstrated Egypt’s sustained capacity to present its priorities internationally. President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi defended downstream security while acknowledging other basin countries’ development rights. sis.gov.eg . That acknowledgment matters. Its practical value, however, depends upon whether upstream development is allowed to alter an unequal distribution of benefits. A right that can be exercised only when existing beneficiaries approve its consequences is precariously close to a privilege granted at their discretion. Cairo’s diplomatic strength lies partly in continuity. Political leaders establish the message; technical institutions elaborate it; diplomats repeat it; conferences and media carry it to wider audiences. Ethiopia should study that discipline. It should also challenge the selective reasoning that can accompany it. The repeated invocation of Egyptian vulnerability does not settle how competing needs should be reconciled. Repetition may establish familiarity, but familiarity is no substitute for an equitable argument. The essential arithmetic is modest: Egypt’s security cannot require Ethiopia’s development to approach zero. Any arrangement built upon that assumption would contain the seeds of its own failure. The basin’s political equation has several populations, several economies and several legitimate claims. A settlement that recognizes only one country’s indispensable needs leaves too many variables outside the calculation. Those excluded interests eventually return as mistrust, resistance and renewed dispute. Ethiopia should therefore begin with the human purpose of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. Electricity means a functioning clinic, a productive workshop, a student able to study after sunset and an enterprise capable of expanding. These aspirations deserve the same moral seriousness as downstream concerns. Poverty should never become the invisible baseline against which another country’s security is measured. An Ethiopian household’s exclusion from reliable power is also a deprivation, even when it produces fewer international headlines. At Tana, Dr. Abiy appropriately connected the dam’s achievement to the obligation to deliver reliable electricity, industrial growth, and improved livelihoods. www.ena.et That is the standard Ethiopian leadership should accept. National achievement acquires lasting authority through public benefit. A dam’s significance rests in the opportunities it creates, and Ethiopia’s international case becomes stronger when its domestic performance makes those opportunities visible. Yet a sound Ethiopian argument must examine operational risks rather than assume that a legitimate purpose resolves them. Reservoir management, prolonged drought and downstream planning require evidence and workable cooperation. Ethiopia should support useful information exchange, credible technical assessment and practical procedures for managing disagreement. Such measures demonstrate responsible authority. They also make it harder to turn uncertainty into an unlimited argument against Ethiopian development. Egypt bears a corresponding responsibility: it must distinguish demonstrable risks from demands that preserve its preferred position indefinitely. A request for dependable drought safeguards deserves serious negotiation. An expectation that upstream development must leave every downstream advantage untouched deserves challenge. Existing use matters, but treating it as an immovable ceiling on everyone else’s future would freeze inequality into the rules of cooperation. The United Nations Watercourses Convention provides an important reference through its principles of equitable and reasonable utilization, cooperation and prevention of significant harm. Applying those principles requires attention to relevant law, agreements and circumstances; citing them does not decide every operational dispute. Their broader significance is clear, however: shared water governance requires consideration of multiple interests. It cannot responsibly be reduced to unlimited upstream discretion or permanent downstream predominance. Ethiopia’s strongest response would combine legal precision with scientific openness. Rainfall totals, for example, reveal little without examining seasonality, storage, accessibility and infrastructure. Equally, claims about a dam’s regional benefits require scrutiny of operating conditions. The country should publish credible analysis, acknowledge uncertainty and invite serious examination. Evidence gives diplomacy a foundation that rhetorical escalation cannot supply. Ethiopia does not need to exaggerate its rights to establish that they matter. Maritime access requires the same discipline. Article 125 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea recognizes access and transit rights for landlocked states while requiring agreement on their exercise and protecting transit states’ legitimate interests. It provides a framework for cooperation, not an automatic entitlement to another country’s territory or a particular port. www.un.org Ethiopia can pursue commercial agreements, infrastructure partnerships, leases and dependable transit arrangements through consent. The Prime Minister’s emphasis on dialogue offers the appropriate political foundation. This makes categorical resistance to Ethiopia’s lawful maritime aspirations especially shortsighted. A dependable corridor can generate port revenue, infrastructure investment, employment, and larger markets. The commercial logic is additive: greater Ethiopian activity can enlarge opportunities for coastal economies. Governments should negotiate the distribution of those gains, rather than assume that Ethiopia’s improved access necessarily diminishes their sovereignty. Properly designed agreements can protect both sovereignty and commercial reliability. Recent coordination among Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan warrants careful Ethiopian assessment. Such alignment does not, by itself, prove a covert strategy of destabilization. Nevertheless, any approach that treats constraining Ethiopia as a durable source of regional advantage would be a grave miscalculation. An economically frustrated and politically insecure Horn would offer Egypt little dependable reassurance. Pressure that deepens mistrust can make the cooperation Cairo seeks harder to obtain. Egypt should resist the temptation to treat every Ethiopian gain as an Egyptian loss. That assumption turns diplomacy into a room with narrowing walls. It encourages tactical obstruction while neglecting the larger interest in a capable upstream partner able to negotiate, share information, and implement commitments. Ethiopia’s instability would make those tasks more difficult. Predictability depends upon institutions, and institutions require a viable economic and political foundation. Ethiopia must draw the corresponding lesson at home. National cohesion, accountable government, and administrative competence strengthen external influence. Its citizens deserve institutions that convert national projects into public opportunity and diplomatic commitments into reliable performance. Confidence abroad becomes more credible when supported by competence at home. The defense of Ethiopian interests therefore requires investment in domestic legitimacy alongside forceful international advocacy. It also requires intellectual infrastructure. Ethiopia needs hydrologists who can test scenarios, lawyers who can explain competing obligations, economists who can evaluate corridor arrangements, and scholars who can assess regional developments independently. A credible research institution devoted to Nile cooperation and the Horn’s economic security could contribute substantially. Its value would depend upon transparent methods and freedom to publish inconvenient findings. Scholarship loses authority when its conclusions are assigned in advance. Universities, professional associations, civil society organizations and diaspora specialists should help sustain that effort. Ethiopia should engage the strongest Egyptian arguments, identify weaknesses in its own policies and produce proposals that withstand scrutiny. Knowledge must accumulate across changes of personnel. A country should not have to reconstruct its case whenever a neighboring minister delivers a speech. Tana can support this continuity by connecting African expertise with the practical responsibilities of government. The continental argument must be equally confident. Pan-Africanism cannot mean preserving an inherited hierarchy in which some societies retain established benefits while others are asked to postpone transformation. Nor can it disregard Egyptian vulnerability. Egypt belongs within the African community whose future Ethiopia invokes. A credible African settlement would protect downstream lives while recognizing upstream development as a legitimate and necessary part of continental progress. Dr. Abiy’s Tana remarks deserve support because they connect an enduring Ethiopian priority to dialogue and mutual benefit. Their promise now requires patient negotiation, technically credible proposals, and agreements that partners can trust. Ethiopia should build upon that foundation to present a coherent regional vision: electricity that supports production, corridors that sustain commerce, and institutions that make cooperation dependable. Cairo can help shape that future, but it must reconsider an approach that too readily confuses Ethiopian advancement with Egyptian danger. The Nile cannot become a permanent instrument for rationing another nation’s aspirations. Ethiopia, for its part, should defend its interests with the confidence to negotiate and the discipline to make its proposals credible. Egypt’s water security deserves protection. Ethiopia’s development deserves room to advance. A durable settlement must be built around both realities. About the Author Mohamud A. Ahmed – Cagaweyne is a Columnist, Political and Security Analyst, Researcher and Greenlight Advisors Group. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia is urged to redefine its diplomatic stance regarding the Nile dispute, which has been dominated by Egypt's narrative of survival. The article emphasizes that Ethiopia's development should not be viewed as a threat but rather as a necessity for its population of over 130 million. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's recent remarks at the Tana High-Level Forum highlight the importance of maritime access for Ethiopia's security and development, framing it as a mutual benefit for regional partners. The author argues that Egypt's historical advantages should not translate into perpetual control over Ethiopia's economic choices. A balanced approach is essential, recognizing both countries' needs and fostering cooperation rather than conflict. The article calls for Ethiopia to present its case with clarity and evidence, advocating for equitable water governance that respects the interests of all basin countries. Ultimately, a collaborative strategy is necessary to ensure regional stability and shared prosperity. (151 words)

ethiopia.title: Ethiopian Passport Ranks Among World's Lowest, Limiting Travel to 17 Visa-Free Destinations
ethiopia.content: Ethiopian Passport Ranks Among World's Lowest, Limiting Travel to 17 Visa-Free Destinations - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopian Passport Ranks Among World's Lowest, Limiting Travel to 17 Visa-Free Destinations Ethiopian Passport Services Ethiopian passport. 26 October 2026 Capital FM (Nairobi) By Bruhan Makong Nairobi — Ethiopian passport holders can travel to only 17 countries without a visa, according to figures attributed to the 2026 Global Passport Power Index, highlighting barriers facing Ethiopian citizens seeking international business, education and cultural opportunities. The index places Ethiopia at position 90 globally, alongside countries including Somalia, Yemen, Syria and Afghanistan, according to the report cited by Passport Rank. Ethiopian citizens can access a further 33 destinations through visas on arrival, while only five African Union member states -- Kenya, Benin, The Gambia, Rwanda and Togo -- are listed as allowing them visa-free entry. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The ranking reflects the restrictions Ethiopian travelers face when seeking to cross borders, with advance visa applications, extensive documentation and processing delays potentially complicating international travel. These barriers can affect businesses seeking to attend trade exhibitions, negotiate deals or build partnerships abroad, as well as students and researchers pursuing academic exchanges and other international opportunities. The report attributes the passport's low standing to a combination of economic conditions, security concerns and diplomatic relations. It says foreign governments commonly consider income levels, security risks, and the likelihood of visa overstays when determining entry requirements. Regional instability and security concerns in the Horn of Africa are also cited as factors contributing to strict visa screening for Ethiopian travelers. The report further points to limited reciprocal visa-waiver arrangements as a constraint on mobility. The restrictions can create challenges for Ethiopian companies seeking to expand internationally, particularly where foreign businesspeople can enter Ethiopia through e-visas or visas on arrival while Ethiopian nationals must undergo more demanding visa procedures to visit potential markets. The report says the consequences extend beyond commerce to academic cooperation, cultural exchanges, and international engagement. Read the original article on Capital FM . ethiopia.title: Ethiopia's Transitional Justice Should Resume, but Not Where It Left Off - allAfrica.com
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia's Transitional Justice Should Resume, but Not Where It Left Off - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia's Transitional Justice Should Resume, but Not Where It Left Off Ninaras / Wikimedia Commons A street scene in Addis Ababa (file photo). 26 October 2026 Institute for Security Studies (Tshwane/Pretoria) analysis By Tadesse Simie Metekia Public consultations on transitional justice laws should start only after National Dialogue recommendations, gaps and new developments have been considered. Ethiopia's Ministry of Justice launched a government-civil society platform on transitional justice on 23 October, signalling the resumption of the process that stalled in April 2025. The transitional justice website is now active, and public consultations on draft transitional justice laws are reportedly expected to begin soon. The interruption came just as the draft laws were about to be opened for consultations . The pause, which had no official explanation, weakened momentum and created uncertainty. To rebuild public and donor confidence, reasons for the resumption should be made public - along with next steps and timelines. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Four priorities should guide the resumed process: the National Dialogue's recommendations, existing gaps, outstanding commitments and developments during the pause. The first priority is the National Dialogue Commission's recommendations , which were submitted to Parliament on 3 October. They are yet to be made public. Since transitional justice was allegedly paused to make way for the dialogue, proceeding without considering its recommendations would miss the point and the chance to strengthen transitional justice. The Ministry of Justice should establish a committee to review the dialogue's implications for the Transitional Justice Policy, draft legislation and implementation. The recommendations may affect transitional justice in three ways: through explicit proposals affecting its scope and mandates; through relevant recommendations in other thematic areas; and through broader reforms that may overlap or interact with its implementation. The review should therefore extend beyond recommendations explicitly labelled as transitional justice. Addressing these implications requires two complementary approaches. Targeted adjustments to the legal frameworks should incorporate relevant recommendations without reopening the entire legal and policy basis for public debate. A separate strategy could coordinate with other institutions or reforms mentioned in the dialogue's recommendations to prevent institutional confusion or another pause. Beyond its specific recommendations, the dialogue could help give Parliament a more prominent role in transitional justice. It may also contribute to establishing a shared, officially recognised account of victimhood and suffering across communities, laying the groundwork for official acknowledgement of and apology for the violence and harm suffered. These contributions should be reflected in the revised transitional justice framework. The second priority is to address unresolved weaknesses in the policy. The existing framework had shortcomings concerning which institution could resolve legal disputes arising between transitional justice bodies. The proposed Special Bench could do this. Accountability for crimes allegedly committed by foreign perpetrators, particularly Eritrean forces during the 2020-2022 Tigray war, also remains insufficiently addressed. Mental health and psychosocial support are hidden under the reparations pillar. The revised framework should recognise them as cross-cutting priorities with clear institutional responsibilities - if not as a standalone pillar whose implementation should begin immediately. Currently, just a few civil society organisations offer support to victims and survivors in their struggle to heal and be recognised. Economic, social and cultural rights violations also require greater attention, not only in reparations but across other pillars such as criminal accountability and institutional reform. Reform should extend beyond vetting security and justice institutions to government offices responsible for economic governance and development, whose policies and practices may have contributed to historical grievances and systemic violations. The process also had procedural gaps regarding participation. Dedicated consultations with youth, diaspora communities and other vulnerable groups and underrepresented constituencies did not take place. This should not be repeated in the forthcoming consultations. For communities excluded by continuing conflicts, the resumed process should provide opportunities for later participation and targeted adjustments. The third priority is fulfilling outstanding commitments. The coordination mechanism envisaged in the policy is yet to be established. Its absence led to failure to resolve misunderstandings between the National Dialogue and transitional justice processes, ultimately contributing to the pause. The urgent need for such a mechanism was also recognised in the 2024 transitional justice implementation roadmap. This called for an interim, multi-stakeholder body to guide and monitor progress until formal transitional justice institutions were established. Establishing this mechanism is now even more important to coordinate transitional justice with institutions and reforms emerging from the dialogue. The fourth priority is to consider how the institutional landscape has evolved during the pause. Regional transitional justice initiatives, including the Commission for Investigation of Violence and Reconciliation and Reparation of Victims in the Somali Region, have advanced their work. During the break, the Commission of Inquiry on Tigray Genocide also released its findings. The national transitional justice framework must clarify its relationship with these initiatives, particularly in recognising and using their findings, institutional cooperation and avoiding duplication. Ethiopia has also established thousands of customary courts across several regions, with the new criminal procedure and evidence code allowing for complementarity between formal and traditional justice mechanisms in criminal cases. But the Transitional Justice Policy addresses traditional justice largely in abstract terms. Its practical integration within each transitional justice pillar, and principles and safeguards governing this relationship, require clarification. To strengthen the independence, transparency and credibility of the forthcoming consultation process, two measures are essential. First, independent experts involved in drafting the laws should participate alongside Ministry of Justice experts to ensure independent scrutiny and preserve the coherence and rationale of the legal frameworks. Second, the draft laws should be shared in advance to allow stakeholders to prepare informed contributions. Resumption should kick off with independent monitoring, parliamentary oversight, African Union engagement and meaningful civil society participation. Civil society's contribution should not be confined to structures controlled by the Justice Ministry or other government institutions. It must retain the space to organise independently, contribute to implementation and exercise critical oversight. Its access to credible information and opportunities for meaningful engagement should not be conditional on membership in a Ministry of Justice-led civil society coordination platform. Overall, the conclusion of the National Dialogue appears to have offered an opportunity to end the uncertainty surrounding transitional justice. The immediate priorities are to review and incorporate those recommendations, address outstanding legal and institutional gaps and commitments, update the roadmap and proceed with consultations on revised legislation. Rather than restarting transitional justice from where the process left off, the task should be to recalibrate and resume. For permission to re-publish ISS Today articles, please email us. ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia's transitional justice process is set to resume after a pause since April 2025, with the Ministry of Justice launching a government-civil society platform on October 23, 2026. However, public consultations on transitional justice laws should only commence after considering the recommendations from the National Dialogue, which were submitted to Parliament on October 3. The previous interruption created uncertainty and weakened momentum, necessitating transparency about the reasons for resuming the process. Key priorities include integrating the National Dialogue's recommendations, addressing existing policy gaps, fulfilling outstanding commitments, and adapting to changes in the institutional landscape during the pause. The process must ensure meaningful participation from civil society and vulnerable groups, while independent experts should be involved in drafting laws to enhance credibility. Overall, the focus should be on recalibrating the transitional justice framework rather than simply picking up where it left off, aiming for a more inclusive and effective approach. (159 words)

(AP Photo) Short Url https://arab.news/p7fd9 Updated 26 October 2026 19:25 afp October 26, 2026 19:22 Follow President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud sent in federal troops to oust the head of South West State Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen Laftagareen has launched repeated attempts to retake the region and its main city of Baidoa Updated 26 October 2026 19:25 afp October 26, 2026 19:22 Follow MOGADISHU: Forces loyal to an ousted regional leader in southwestern Somalia again clashed with federal soldiers near the outskirts of Baidoa city, officials and witnesses said Monday. Several states in the deeply fragmented country are opposed to control by President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, and in March his government sent in troops to oust the head of South West State, Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen. He has launched repeated attempts to retake the region and its main city of Baidoa, most recently in September when thousands of his forces attacked, leaving at least three people dead. The fighting erupted as Somali security forces established new defensive positions in Burjeedka, a small settlement near the city. “A large-scale operation targeting terrorist groups began this morning,” South West State’s information minister Nur Siidow Baaba told reporters. He said federal forces were advancing in several directions “to restore state authority in areas recently lost.” “We inflicted heavy casualties, while two of our soldiers were killed,” said Somali army commander Abdullahi Hassan. But a pro-Laftagareen commander, Hassan Abdulkadir Mohamed, claimed his forces were in control. “A unit of our Darwiish forces clashed with enemy troops from Mogadishu, forcing them into a humiliating retreat to Baidoa,” he said, without providing more details. Witnesses in Baidoa reported hearing heavy fighting along the road to Mogadishu early on Monday. “We heard loud explosions and saw a convoy of reinforcements leaving the city toward the fighting. Gunfire continued for more than an hour,” said resident Nur Yare. The full casualty toll remains unknown, although both sides acknowledged losses in the clash. Last week, at least three members of a pro-Laftagareen militia were killed by airstrikes in the Wajid district, Bakool region. somalia.summary: In southern Somalia, regional forces loyal to ousted leader Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen clashed with federal troops near Baidoa city. This conflict follows President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's deployment of federal troops in March to remove Laftagareen from power. Despite previous attempts to regain control, including a significant assault in September that resulted in casualties, Laftagareen's forces continue to challenge the federal government. On Monday, fighting intensified as Somali security forces established new defensive positions in Burjeedka, with both sides claiming to have inflicted losses on the other. Witnesses reported heavy gunfire and explosions, indicating a fierce confrontation. The situation remains fluid, with the full extent of casualties yet to be determined. The ongoing clashes highlight the deep fragmentation and instability within Somalia, as various regions resist central government authority.

somalia.title: Villa Somalia Touts 1.8 Million Voter Registrations as Opposition Rejects Electoral Process - FTL Somalia
somalia.content: Villa Somalia Touts 1.8 Million Voter Registrations as Opposition Rejects Electoral Process - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Politics Villa Somalia Touts 1.8 Million Voter Registrations as Opposition Rejects Electoral Process October 26, 2026 4 min read MOGADISHU , Villa Somalia has released detailed figures on its electoral process, announcing that 1,824,853 citizens have registered to vote across 1,102 polling stations in 50 of the 92 districts that existed in 1991, and that 1,435 officials have been elected directly by the people. The figures were shared by the Presidency’s official account , quoting President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, who has repeatedly framed the introduction of one-person, one-vote elections as Somalia’s return to a democratic path abandoned 57 years ago. The president has also claimed that “not a single armed incident occurred at any polling station across the country” and commended politicians who accepted the results despite their disagreements. A Partial Picture The president’s numbers are technically accurate for the districts where voting has taken place, notably in South West State, Galmudug, Hirshabelle, and the Banadir region. In Hirshabelle, the Justice and Solidarity Party secured 78 of 99 parliamentary seats with 114,633 votes cast, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the election results . But the figures describe a process that remains incomplete and deeply contested. The 50 districts covered represent just over half of the 92 districts that existed in 1991. More importantly, the opposition Somali Future Council, which includes the Puntland and Jubaland administrations, has rejected the federal government’s electoral timetable and the constitutional amendments that extended the president’s term. The opposition has not rejected direct elections as a principle. It has rejected the process by which they are being implemented, arguing that major decisions on elections should be reached through dialogue and consensus rather than unilateral action. The Somali Future Council has stated it is ready for “genuine dialogue to reach an electoral agreement and a realistic, implementable timetable,” but has demanded that the president halt what it describes as unilateral measures. The Timing of the Announcement Villa Somalia’s decision to release these figures now, rather than waiting for the National Consultative Forum it has invited the opposition to attend from November 14 to 18, is politically significant. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the invitation , the government has extended a formal invitation to Nabad iyo Nolol, the Somali Future Council, the National Unity Forum, and the Civil Society Coalition to discuss federal election matters. But by presenting the electoral process as a success with concrete numbers before those talks begin, the president is establishing facts on the ground. The implicit argument is that if 1.8 million Somalis have registered and 1,435 officials have been elected, the process has a legitimacy that its opponents cannot deny. Those who reject it are rejecting the will of the people. Critical Note The figures are real, but they are not the whole story. A process can produce real votes and real officials while still being politically contested. The JSP’s victories in Hirshabelle and Galmudug were achieved in elections that the principal opposition parties either boycotted or were excluded from. The Galmudug rerun excluded Towfiiq, the party that had successfully challenged the original vote in court. The Hirshabelle vote proceeded despite the Xawaadle clan’s declaration that it would not accept any election without a prior political agreement. The president’s claim that no armed incidents occurred at polling stations may be technically true in some districts, but it ignores the armed Macawiisley fighters who seized voter registration centres in Beledweyne, the curfews and security restrictions that accompanied the votes, and the broader political violence engulfing South West State, where Laftagareen-aligned forces are fighting federal troops. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the political crisis , Puntland President Said Abdullahi Deni has warned that Somali statehood is at risk and called for urgent national dialogue. The real test of the government’s electoral project is not the number of registered voters or elected officials. It is whether the process can produce a result that the opposition and the regional administrations are willing to accept. The November forum is the government’s opportunity to demonstrate that it is serious about consensus. Releasing triumphalist statistics before the talks begin suggests the opposite. It suggests that the government sees the forum not as a negotiation, but as a ratification exercise. If that is the case, the figures will not resolve the crisis. They will deepen it. President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud emphasized this achievement as a step towards restoring democracy after 57 years, claiming no armed incidents occurred during the voting process. However, the opposition, particularly the Somali Future Council, has rejected the electoral process, arguing that it lacks legitimacy due to the exclusion of major political parties and the absence of a consensus-driven approach. They demand a halt to what they view as unilateral actions by the government and are open to genuine dialogue to establish an electoral agreement. The timing of the government's announcement, ahead of a planned National Consultative Forum, raises concerns that it aims to solidify its position rather than engage in meaningful negotiations. The situation remains tense, with warnings from regional leaders about the potential risks to Somali statehood if consensus is not achieved.

Facebook Instagram X VKontakte Youtube Somali Guardian News Somalia Africa World Featured Editor Picks Editorials Home News Somalia Fighting erupts near Baidoa as Somali army advance on Burhakabo stalls Fighting erupts near Baidoa as Somali army advance on Burhakabo stalls October 26, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Heavy fighting erupted on Monday on the outskirts of Baidoa between the Somali National Army and forces loyal to Abdiaziz Laftagareen, the former president of Southwest State. An official from Laftagareen’s faction said army units had been ambushed on the road. The soldiers were travelling through the Burjed area, near Baidoa, reportedly on their way to Burhakabo. The town lies 60km east of Baidoa and was recently seized from the federal government by Laftagareen’s forces. The official said their fighters attacked because the soldiers wanted to pose for photographs on the edge of Baidoa and then claim to have carried out an operation. Laftagareen’s group said it killed dozens of soldiers and destroyed a number of military vehicles. Neither figure has been independently confirmed. The federal government and its ally, the current Southwest State administration, have not yet responded. The clashes come as militant attacks continue to stall about 2,000 Somali troops who set out on Saturday from Baledogle airfield, on the Mogadishu-Baidoa road, to retake Burhakabo and other towns in the Bay region that Laftagareen’s forces recently captured. The troops, travelling with more than 200 military vehicles, are now stranded in Leego, about 50km east of Burhakabo and close to Baledogle airfield. Reports indicate that the militant group Al-Shabaab has mined the entire road. On Saturday, local media reported that Al-Shabaab ambushed the convoy, sparking hours of fighting that caused casualties on both sides. The army said it gained the upper hand and killed seven militants. Al-Shabaab-affiliated media reported that 10 soldiers were killed and four military vehicles destroyed. Local media say the advance has stalled mainly because of fears of landmines and further ambushes. Residents said security forces ordered them to leave Leego, warning that the town could be hit by Turkish air strikes. Leego is currently held by the Somali military, with militants positioned on its outskirts. The federal government is seeking to consolidate its control of Southwest State, where it installed a loyal administration led by former parliament speaker Adan Madobe. It ousted regional President Abdiasis Mohamed Hassan Laftagareen in March in a military offensive backed by Turkish air power. Staff Reporter GAROWE ONLINE Posted On 26-10-2026, 12:13PM MOGADISHU — Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud whose presidential term expired in May 2026 travelled to Uganda hours after inviting opposition groups and the leaders of the semi-autonomous states of Puntland and Jubaland to talks next month aimed at addressing a deepening dispute over federal elections. The timing of the trip comes as political and constitutional tensions intensify in Somalia, particularly over the president’s term in office and the country’s electoral system. During a meeting in Entebbe in August 2026, Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni reportedly pressed Hassan Sheikh to engage with Somali opposition groups and seek a negotiated settlement to the country’s growing political crisis. Museveni was also reported to have warned that Uganda could withdraw its troops from Somalia if the government failed to reach an agreement with political stakeholders opposed to its proposed electoral system. The opposition has accused the administration of pursuing an electoral framework that has deepened political divisions and created uncertainty over the country’s democratic transition. Uganda is a major troop contributor to the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), which supports Somali security forces in their fight against Al-Shabaab, the Al-Qaeda-linked militant group. Kampala is concerned that a prolonged political deadlock in Mogadishu could distract the government and security institutions from counterinsurgency operations and undermine the stability of the African Union mission. Although the Somali presidency has not publicly confirmed that the latest trip is directly linked to the election dispute or Uganda’s reported concerns, its timing has drawn attention to Kampala’s potential role in efforts to ease the political crisis. Museveni has reportedly urged Somali leaders to engage in inclusive dialogue, stressing the need for a political settlement that would allow the country to maintain its security gains and strengthen state institutions. Uganda has also emphasised the importance of building a capable Somali national army that can eventually assume full responsibility for the country’s security as African Union forces withdraw. The transition is part of broader plans to transfer security duties to Somali forces by 2027. Museveni has expressed concern that Ugandan troops could face continued risks while Somali political leaders remain divided over the distribution of power and the electoral process. Uganda has played a central role in international security efforts in Somalia for years, with its troops forming a key part of the African Union’s military presence. The political dispute therefore carries implications beyond the electoral process, potentially affecting the fight against Al-Shabaab and plans to transfer security responsibilities to Somali forces. Hassan Sheikh’s invitation to opposition leaders and the subsequent trip to Uganda come at a sensitive moment for Somalia, as efforts to reach an agreement over elections face competing political demands and uncertainty over the country’s constitutional future. His presidential term expired in May 2026, and he has invited opposition groups and leaders from Puntland and Jubaland for talks to address these issues. The timing of his visit is significant, as Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni has urged him to engage with opposition factions and seek a resolution to the political crisis. Museveni has warned that Uganda may withdraw its troops from Somalia if a consensus is not reached, raising concerns about the stability of the African Union mission against Al-Shabaab. The ongoing political deadlock not only threatens Somalia's democratic transition but also impacts security operations, as Uganda plays a crucial role in supporting Somali forces. The situation remains delicate, with the potential for significant implications for Somalia's future governance and security landscape.

somalia.summary: The climate crisis is severely impacting Somalia, leading to widespread hunger among its population. Currently, approximately 5.4 million people in the country are facing food insecurity, primarily due to prolonged drought conditions that have devastated livestock, which many Somalis rely on for their livelihoods. Mohamed Abdi, the Somalia country director for the Norwegian Refugee Council, emphasizes the dire situation, highlighting that the ongoing climate challenges are exacerbating existing vulnerabilities. The combination of climate change and its effects on agriculture and livestock is creating a humanitarian crisis, necessitating urgent international attention and assistance. As the situation worsens, the need for sustainable solutions to address both immediate food needs and long-term climate resilience becomes increasingly critical for the affected communities in Somalia.

This meeting, held in Mogadishu, brought together various government institutions and the management of the Port of Mogadishu to discuss the policy framework that will guide the development and management of maritime transport in Somalia. This initiative reflects Somalia's commitment to developing its maritime infrastructure and ensuring effective management of its ports, which are vital for trade and economic development.

Photograph: Jonathan Torgovnik/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A colonel from US special operations in Somalia with a soldier from a branch of the Somali army trained by US special forces, in Mogadishu in 2023. Photograph: Jonathan Torgovnik/Getty Images Global development US forces accused of ‘weaponising’ Somalia’s floods by trapping women and children in the path of El Niño Exclusive: Coordinated airstrikes on territory held by al-Shabaab are driving the civilian population to find refuge alongside a river where rising water levels are a threat to safety. Is it a deliberate military strategy? Supported by About this content Mark Townsend in Kismayo Mon 26 Oct 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 07.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google T he water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her home, five metres from the flooded River Juba in southern Somalia , never stood a chance. There was nowhere to go. Ali’s city of Jilib was under attack. Repeated airstrikes, said the mother of six, were pinning its population beside the rising river. “The drones come all the time,” said the 27-year-old. “We hear them constantly. They kill animals, civilians. The town is big but destruction is everywhere.” View image in fullscreen Cayni Ali with her child Mandeq at a health centre in Kismayo, Somalia. Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham Asho Omar from Malenda, a village near Jilib, described “constant” airstrikes that had forced people towards the banks of the Juba. “The airstrikes are everywhere; it is difficult to move. So many people have been killed.” Their testimony offers a rare glimpse of life inside the stronghold of al-Shabaab , the Islamist militants who control 30% of Somalia. Closed off from the outside world, residents describe a city dealing with significant civilian casualties. Bodies, some said, lay in the streets. The ongoing conflict is a legally ambiguous, shadowy war coordinated by the United States in east Africa , in which there is little accountability for harm to Somali civilians. The United States Africa Command (Africom) would not share “operational security” details of a seemingly accelerating campaign that has also raised questions over potential covert US strikes. But there is, perhaps, an even darker dimension to the offensive on al-Shabaab’s de facto capital . Sources say the military strategy appears to be seeking to drown those living in al-Shabaab territory by “weaponising” a rapidly strengthening El Niño , forecast to intensify Somalia’s rainy season from this month. View image in fullscreen An aerial view of the Juba River, close to the town of Kismayo. Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham “The airstrikes are forcing people to go close to the river. It’s an extremely aggressive offensive, exploiting El Niño as a weapon of war to push the population into flood-prone areas,” said a source monitoring the Juba floodplain in southern Somalia. Pinning the population – which includes large numbers of women and children – on the river’s floodplain has raised concerns of large-scale deaths in the months ahead. “The official line is that they are targeting military positions and al-Shabaab, but because al-Shabaab is embedded within the community, it’s difficult to avoid collateral damage,” added the source. When El Niño last struck Somalia in 2023, it caused the worst floods seen in the country for a century, displacing more than 1.2 million people . Analysts have questioned the ethics of the US military allegedly using mapping data from flood-prone areas – conceived to mitigate civilian casualties – to inflict harm. Jethro Norman, a senior researcher with the Danish Institute for International Studies , said: “A weaponisation of El Niño is a reversal of process – using humanitarian remote sensing to inflict casualties rather than to mitigate harm. You capture the cumulative impact of a sustained airstrikes campaign in an El Niño flooding context.” View image in fullscreen The aftermath of the 2023 El Niño in Luuq district, Jubaland, which caused the worst floods ever seen in the country. Photograph: Feisal Omar/Reuters US officials deny exploiting climatic factors. A spokesperson said: “Africom does not target civilians, conduct operations for the purpose of displacing civilian populations or use weather or flooding as a method of warfare. Africom targets lawful military objectives and takes feasible measures to mitigate civilian harm.” Nevertheless, many wonder if the opportunity to weaken al-Shabaab using the weather was too tempting to ignore, offering a catastrophic drowning event blamed on a supercharged El Niño . L ike many cities, Jilib’s location has been found wanting in an era of extreme weather. On a low-lying plain, the city is chronically vulnerable to flooding. In 2023, vast swathes of farmland were submerged. Halimo Abdikadir from Kamsuuma, south of Jillib, described the destruction of her home, 6 miles (10km) from the river. “The waters came quickly at night – when they left, everything was mud. A lot of animals drowned.” Arbey Famu from Ahmed Yare, another village outside Jilib, expects this El Niño to be far worse than 2023 : her crops of maize and sorghum are underwater. “In Jilib, there is big flooding already,” said the 70-year-old. US defence officials will know the early indicators of El Niño’s impact in al-Shabaab’s heartland. UN agencies say the Juba River basin is of “particular concern”. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) , meanwhile, foresees “severe flooding”. View image in fullscreen Arbey Abdi Famu, a resident of the Dalhiska displacement camp in Kismayo. Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham Attacking Jilib using ground forces carries much risk. Airstrikes can yield triumphs such as the death of a senior al-Shabaab commander on 1 October, but are unable to overrun a city of 100,000. Ali Adan Ali, the commissioner for displaced people in Jubaland , is worried. In his Kismayo office, Ali identified 327 regions prone to flooding. By October, El Niño warnings had only been issued to half. His chief concern is the lack of boats. Without them, he says, thousands in al-Shabaab territory risk being trapped on the east side of the river, unable to reach help in Kismayo, at the mouth of the Juba. View image in fullscreen People on the streets of Kismayo, where long-term drought and USAID cuts have brought misery. Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham Three years ago, during the last El Niño, Ali says, 19,000 people were stranded for a week without food. “We are running out of time,” he says. The absence of boats sums up Somalia’s funding woes. In 2023, the country’s aid budget was $2.2bn. Now it stands at about $300,000. Flood protection investment has dwindled. Compounding concerns is al-Shabaab’s lack of preparedness in the area it controls. Ali has not received a response from the militants regarding El Niño readiness. Cayni Ali said there are no sandbags or flood defences deployed yet in Jilib. Earth walls were erected along the river but have proved insufficient. “They are not big enough,” she said. The latest flood advisory for the River Juba urges communities to “reinforce” weak riverbanks. C orroborating testimonies describe a prolonged – and seemingly indiscriminate – campaign of airstrikes against al-Shabaab that appears to have killed many civilians. The US would not share details of potential civilian fatalities “to protect US and partner forces and preserve operational security”. Farhan Ahmed, who lived in Jilib until fleeing last month, described constant terror. “There were airstrikes every day, all the time.” One strike flattened five homes in his neighbourhood. Ahmed, 35, described bodies littering the city streets. Fadumo Abdi claimed the airstrikes were largely failing to target militants. “The attacks are mostly killing civilians. Some were buried, but some were not,” she said. Abdikadir, from Kamsuuma, added: “The drone attacks on Jilib are too much. So many people die.” Yusuf Siidi, 27, from Araare near Jamame in al-Shabaab territory, witnessed three teenagers killed in one strike. Maryan Salah was at home near Jamame when a drone sent a shard of burning metal 20cm long into her back yard, landing next to her two-year-old daughter. “ It was so close. I am very angry. I’m not part of the conflict.” Salah’s near miss predates the current offensive. She can recall only that it happened in “mid-March”. The US admits a drone strike near Jamame on 19 March, but no other data is provided. View image in fullscreen A mother takes her baby to a Somalia Red Crescent Society health centre in Kismayo to check for symptoms of malnutrition. Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham Although eyewitness accounts detail an extraordinary number of strikes in Jilib, official US records confirm only one airstrike in Jilib during August. Six took place last month. Between the start of August and now, the US says it conducted a total of just 11 strikes. Allegations of ambiguity increasingly characterise US operations in Somalia. It is an opaque approach that raises questions over whether Africom has authorised covert airstrikes in the region. Records from the nearest hospital indicate intensive airstrikes or fighting. The ICRC has treated 205 patients with “weapon-related” injuries in Kismayo this year, a 43% increase on last year. David Sterman, analyst at the New America thinktank, said: “The possibility that we are seeing covert US strikes always looms large when there are strikes without clear attribution.” View image in fullscreen A malnourished three-month-old baby in Kismayo hospital’s intensive-care ward in September. Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham The US, however, said it publicised “all airstrikes conducted under its authority in Somalia. We do not maintain an undisclosed or unannounced strike count.” Turkey has also used drones to target al-Shabaab in Somalia. Operating alongside Africom, Turkey rarely divulges any details of its strikes or military operations in Somalia. Beyond airstrikes and floods, the primary concern for Somalis is hunger . Those fleeing the Juba valley – local authorities are offering humanitarian help to those who escape – say there is insufficient food to sustain them. Omar’s family of 13 survives on one fish a day. How big is the fish? Omar held her hands less than 30cm apart. Habiba Ali, 55, from Jamame, said her family – like many – shares one daily meal of maize. Time in between is spent hiding from conflict. “When the fighting stops, we wait for it start again.” In Kismayo, too, long-term drought and USAID cuts have brought misery. Shukri Ahmed, 32, the president of Galbeed refugee camp, estimates that 6,000 might have died in Kismayo’s network of displacement sites since the Trump administration abruptly shut USAID last year. Overnight, two children had died in makeshift shelters from diarrhoea. El Niño will “deepen [Somalia’s] hunger levels”, warns the UN-backed body responsible for identifying famine. Zakaria Mohammed, head nurse at Kismayo’s ICRC-supported hospital for five years, says children from al-Shabaab territory arrive every day so severely malnourished or weak they cannot be saved. Cases of child malnutrition rates have risen 40% this year. Xaawo Nacdoor made it just in time. Al-Shabaab had blocked her leaving Jamame to receive treatment for her baby. But her 14-month-old daughter Faadumo was dying, so Nacdoor fled at night. View image in fullscreen Fadumo Abdi with her 14-month-old baby, Maryan, in the infant intensive-care unit in Kismayo hospital. Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham For three days, with just a bottle of water, Nacdoor walked with her daughter strapped to her back. On the second day, the toddler lost consciousness. “She was severely dehydrated, but I kept going.” Arriving at the hospital, Faadumo weighed 4.1kg. Three days later: 4.4kg. She survived. Most patients here vow never to return home, saying life under al-Shabaab meant no school, education, healthcare or food. For the thousands of families straddling the Juba River – often the poorest – things are about to get much worse. somalia.summary: US forces in Somalia are facing accusations of "weaponising" the country's floods amid a military campaign against the Islamist group al-Shabaab. Reports indicate that coordinated airstrikes are forcing civilians to seek refuge near the flood-prone River Juba, exacerbating their vulnerability as El Niño intensifies the rainy season. Eyewitness accounts describe a relentless barrage of airstrikes, leading to significant civilian casualties and destruction in towns like Jilib. Critics argue that the US military strategy appears to exploit the flooding to weaken al-Shabaab, raising ethical concerns about the use of humanitarian data for military purposes. While US officials deny targeting civilians or using weather as a weapon, the situation remains dire, with insufficient flood defenses and a lack of humanitarian aid. The International Committee of the Red Cross warns of severe flooding, and local authorities express concern over the potential for large-scale displacement and loss of life as conditions worsen.

أفريقيا، بعد تجاوزه لخصمه أسيك ميموزا العاجي. وعاد المغرب الفاسي، بطل الدوري المغربي للموسم الماضي، من العاصمة أبيدجان بالفوز 1-2، ليتأهل لدور المجموعات بعد تعادله ذهاباً في مكناس 1-1. وبعد شوط أول سلبي، تقدم المغرب الفاسي بهدف الكونغولي كريستوفر إيبايي، قبل أن يعادل كيفين باكارا النتيجة لأسيك، وبينما تتجه المواجهة لركلات الترجيح، أحرز خالد بابا هدف الفوز القاتل للمغرب الفاسي في الدقيقة السابعة من الوقت بدل الضائع. ولحق بذلك المغرب الفاسي بمواطنه ووصيفه نهضة بركان الذي أقصى ستار سبورت أكاديمي السيراليوني بالفوز عليه ذهاباً وإياباً. الهلال السوداني هزم سيداما بونا الإثيوبي وتأهل لمجموعات أبطال أفريقيا (نادي الهلال) وفي العاصمة الرواندية كيغالي، التي يتخذها الهلال السوداني ملعباً بيتياً، كرر الهلال فوزه على ضيفه سيداما بونا الإثيوبي 2-صفر، وهي نتيجة الذهاب نفسها لمصلحة الهلال، ليتأهل الفريق السوداني لدور المجموعات. وجاءت ثنائية الهلال في الشوط الأول بواسطة كل من إرنست لوزولو في الدقيقة 33 ومحمد عبد الرحمن «الغربال» في الوقت بدل الضائع للشوط. وبذلك يعوّض الهلال خروج مواطنه ومنافسه التقليدي المريخ، الذي ودّع المسابقة السبت على يد حوريا الغيني بركلات الترجيح. وفي وقت سابق، حسم سيمبا التنزاني تأهله بفوزه 3 - صفر على 15 أوغوستو القادم من غينيا الاستوائية ليتفوق بنتيجة 9 - 1 في مجموع المباراتين، وتأهل كولومب الكاميروني بعد فوزه 1 - صفر على تينغيت السنغالي عقب تفوقه 2 - صفر في الذهاب. مواضيع الرياضة كرة القدم دوري أبطال أفريقيا أخبار المغرب أخبار السودان ساحل العاج الأكثر براتس، مدرب فريق الشمال القطري، صعوبة المواجهة المرتقبة أمام الهلال، مشيراً إلى أنه يدرك الفوارق التاريخية والخبرة التي يمتلكها الفريق السعودي، لكنه شدد في الوقت ذاته على قدرة لاعبيه على تقديم أداء تنافسي والسعي إلى الخروج بنتيجة إيجابية. وقال براتس، خلال المؤتمر الصحافي الذي يسبق المواجهة، إن التحضيرات تسير بالطريقة المعتادة، رغم ضيق الوقت في ظل توالي المباريات، مضيفاً: «نعلم قوة الهلال وخبرة مدربه ولاعبيه، لكننا نملك الرغبة في تقديم كل ما لدينا». وأشار مدرب الشمال إلى أن فريقه يخوض مشاركته الأولى في البطولة، عادّاً أن امتلاك مجموعة من اللاعبين الجيدين يمنحه القدرة على المنافسة، شريطة إظهار إمكاناتهم داخل الملعب، وقال: «ندرك الفارق الكبير في تاريخ الفريقين، ونحترم الهلال ولاعبيه، لكننا نملك لاعبين جيدين، ويجب أن يظهروا إمكاناتهم حتى نتمكن من تحقيق الفوز». وتطرق براتس إلى أهمية انضمام النجم الجزائري رياض محرز إلى صفوف الفريق، موضحاً أن وجوده يمنح الشمال جودة إضافية وقوة وثقة أكبر، ويساعده على منافسة الفرق القوية في البطولة، مشدداً على أهمية امتلاك لاعبين مميزين لخوض مثل هذه الاستحقاقات. وعن الغيابات المحتملة في صفوف الهلال، رأى براتس أن الفرق الكبيرة لا تتأثر عادة بغياب لاعب أو اثنين، لافتاً إلى أن فريقه يعاني بدوره من غياب عدد من اللاعبين، لكنه يمتلك البدائل القادرة على تعويضهم. من جانبه، أكد يوسف سابالي، لاعب الشمال، صعوبة المواجهة أمام الهلال، قائلاً: «نعلم أن المباراة ستكون صعبة أمام فريق كبير، وسنقدم كل ما نملك لتحقيق الفوز». مواضيع دوري أبطال آسيا قطر football.summary: تأهل فريقا المغرب الفاسي والهلال السوداني إلى دور المجموعات في دوري أبطال أفريقيا بعد تحقيقهما انتصارات مهمة في مباريات الإياب. حيث تمكن المغرب الفاسي من الفوز على أسيك ميموزا العاجي بنتيجة 2-1 في أبيدجان، بعد أن تعادل الفريقان في مباراة الذهاب 1-1. سجل أهداف المغرب الفاسي كريستوفر إيبايي وخالد بابا، الذي أحرز هدف الفوز في الدقيقة السابعة من الوقت بدل الضائع. من جهة أخرى، حقق الهلال السوداني فوزاً مريحاً على سيداما بونا الإثيوبي بنتيجة 2-0، ليكرر نتيجة الذهاب. سجل إرنست لوزولو ومحمد عبد الرحمن "الغربال" أهداف الهلال في الشوط الأول. هذا التأهل يعوض الهلال خروج منافسه التقليدي المريخ من البطولة. كما تأهل سيمبا التنزاني وكولومب الكاميروني بعد انتصاراتهما في مبارياتهما.

السوداني سيداما بونا الدوري السوداني الممتاز كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin أضفنا الى 'غوغل' أعرب مدرب الهلال، جوزيف زينباور، عن سعادته بتأهل فريقه إلى دور المجموعات في دوري أبطال أفريقيا، عقب تفوقه على سيداما بونا الإثيوبي بنتيجة 4-0 في مجموع مباراتي الذهاب والإياب بالدور التمهيدي الثاني. وفي مقطع فيديو نشره الموقع الرسمي للنادي، أكد زينباور أن العمل الشاق بدأ فعليًا بعد تحقيق الهدف الأول المتمثل في بلوغ دور المجموعات، مشيرًا إلى ضغط جدول المباريات في الدوري الرواندي. كما شدد على ضرورة معالجة مشكلة إهدار الفرص، التي ظهرت خلال مواجهتي الفريق أمام منافسه الإثيوبي. زينباور: تجاوزنا ظروفًا صعبة وحققنا هدفنا أشاد مدرب الهلال جوزيف زينباور بأداء لاعبيه في مباراتي الذهاب والإياب أمام الفريق الإثيوبي، وخصّ خط الدفاع بالثناء، قائلًا: "حققنا نتيجة إيجابية، وفزنا في المواجهتين وقدمنا أداء متميزًا رغم سوء أرضية الملعب التي تأثرت بضغط المباريات. أعتقد أننا أنجزنا المهمة بنجاح". وأضاف: "ينتظرنا عمل شاق قبل انطلاق مرحلة مجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا ، إذ سنواجه منافسين أقوياء، لذا علينا الاستعداد بصورة مثالية. أنا أثق في لاعبي فريقي وقدرتهم على تقديم مستويات رفيعة، ونترقب نتائج القرعة لنتحدث في حينها". اقرأ أيضًا الهلال يجدد تفوقه على سيداما ويحجز مقعده بمجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا 2026-27 صدم أنديته.. اتحاد الكرة السوداني يحدد موعد انطلاقة الدوري زينباور يشيد بلاعبي الهلال ويستعد لجدول مزدحم وأكد زينباور جاهزية فريقه للتعامل مع ازدحام المباريات في الدوري الرواندي ، قائلًا: "سنخوض 3 مباريات قوية في غضون أسبوع واحد فقط، وأنا أمتلك مجموعة جيدة من اللاعبين. سنصب تركيزنا حاليًا على التحديات المحلية، وبعدها لكل حادث حديث فيما يخص مرحلة المجموعات". وأضاف: "تركيزي منصب على إعداد الفريق بشكل أمثل، وثقتي كبيرة في جميع اللاعبين، وخاصة عناصر خط الدفاع بعد ظهورهم المتميز في مباريات الدورين التمهيديين الأول والثاني من البطولة". ووجّه المدرب الألماني، الذي يخوض موسمه الأول مع الهلال، الشكر إلى جميع العاملين في النادي، مشيدًا بالجهود التي بذلوها لتوفير الظروف المناسبة للفريق. وقال في هذا السياق: "لقد أنجز الجميع عملًا متقنًا، ويتعين علينا أن نثني على ما قدموه لنا من مساعدات، وأخص بالتقدير جماهير النادي التي قدمت دعمًا كبيرًا لفريقها، كما دعمتني بصورة شخصية، وأعدهم بتقديم الأفضل مستقبلًا". النشرة البريدية اشترك معنا بالنشرة البريدية لتصلك آخر أخبار الرياضة اشترك football.summary: أعرب مدرب الهلال السوداني، جوزيف زينباور، عن سعادته بتأهل فريقه إلى دور المجموعات في دوري أبطال أفريقيا بعد الفوز على سيداما بونا الإثيوبي بنتيجة 4-0 في مجموع المباراتين. وأكد زينباور أن العمل الشاق بدأ بعد تحقيق هذا الهدف، مشيرًا إلى التحديات التي تواجه الفريق بسبب ضغط جدول المباريات في الدوري الرواندي. كما أشار إلى ضرورة معالجة مشكلة إهدار الفرص التي ظهرت خلال المباريات السابقة. وأشاد بأداء لاعبيه، خاصة خط الدفاع، رغم الظروف الصعبة مثل سوء أرضية الملعب. زينباور أكد أيضًا جاهزية الفريق لمواجهة المنافسين الأقوياء في مرحلة المجموعات، مع التركيز على الاستعداد المثالي. كما شكر جميع العاملين في النادي والجماهير على دعمهم، مؤكدًا التزامه بتقديم الأفضل في المستقبل.

football.title: الأفريقي التونسي والمغرب الفاسي والهلال السوداني إلى مجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا - شبكة مصدر الاخبارية
football.content: الأفريقي التونسي والمغرب الفاسي والهلال السوداني إلى مجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا - شبكة مصدر الاخبارية الرئيسية فلسطينيو 48 شؤون إسرائيلية عربية وإقليمية اقتصاد تكنولوجيا تقارير خاصة رياضة منوعات إتصل بنا الرئيسية رياضة الأفريقي التونسي والمغرب الفاسي والهلال السوداني إلى مجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا نواذيبو الموريتاني يعوض خسارة الذهاب ويبلغ الدور المقبل.. وقرعة المجموعات تُجرى الأربعاء المقبل الأفريقي التونسي والمغرب الفاسي والهلال السوداني إلى مجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا 26 أكتوبر 2026 12:00 ص وكالات - واصل الأفريقي التونسي مشواره في دوري أبطال أفريقيا لكرة القدم، بعدما حجز بطاقة التأهل إلى مرحلة المجموعات بفوزه على ضيفه تي بي مازيمبي، بطل الكونغو الديمقراطية، بهدف دون رد، الأحد، في إياب الدور التمهيدي الثاني للمسابقة. وسجل الكاميروني تاديوس نكينغ هدف المباراة الوحيد في الدقيقة الثانية من الوقت المحتسب بدلاً من الضائع للشوط الأول، ليمنح الفريق التونسي انتصاراً ثميناً على أرضه، بعد مواجهة اتسمت بأهمية كبيرة للطرفين. وكانت مباراة الذهاب، التي أُقيمت في مدينة لومومباشي الكونغولية الأسبوع الماضي، قد انتهت بالتعادل 1-1، ليحسم الأفريقي التأهل بمجموع المباراتين بنتيجة 2-1. وبهذا الإنجاز، أصبح الأفريقي الممثل الثاني للكرة التونسية في مرحلة المجموعات هذا الموسم، إلى جانب غريمه التقليدي الترجي التونسي، فيما تبخرت آمال مازيمبي في مواصلة مشواره نحو اللقب السادس في تاريخه، والأول منذ عام 2015. ويطمح الأفريقي إلى استعادة أمجاده القارية والمنافسة على لقبه الثاني في البطولة، بعدما سبق له التتويج بدوري أبطال أفريقيا عام 1991. نواذيبو الموريتاني يقلب تأخره ويعبر إلى المرحلة الرئيسية وفي العاصمة الموريتانية نواكشوط، انتزع نواذيبو بطاقة التأهل إلى مرحلة المجموعات، بعدما تغلب على ضيفه سان بيدرو الإيفواري بنتيجة 2-0، على ملعب «شيخ ولد بيديا»، في إياب الدور التمهيدي الثاني. وبدأ الفريق الموريتاني المواجهة بقوة، وافتتح كارتييه ديمبيلي التسجيل في الدقيقة العاشرة، ليمنح أصحاب الأرض تقدماً مبكراً أعاد المواجهة إلى نقطة التعادل في مجموع المباراتين. وفي الدقيقة 53، أضاف شيخ خطاب الهدف الثاني لنواذيبو، ليعزز فرص فريقه في حسم بطاقة التأهل ويمنحه الأفضلية اللازمة بعد خسارة مباراة الذهاب بنتيجة 2-1 خارج أرضه. وبهذا الفوز، عوض نواذيبو خسارته في اللقاء الأول، ليتفوق بنتيجة 3-2 في مجموع المباراتين، ويواصل حضوره في المنافسات القارية، بعدما نجح في استثمار عاملي الأرض والجمهور لحسم المواجهة. ويمثل التأهل خطوة مهمة للنادي الموريتاني، الذي نجح في تجاوز عقبة منافس إيفواري بعد مواجهة امتدت حساباتها إلى المباراتين، ليحجز مكانه بين أندية مرحلة المجموعات. المغرب الفاسي يحسم التأهل بهدف قاتل في أبيدجان بدوره، تأهل المغرب الفاسي إلى مرحلة المجموعات، بعدما حقق فوزاً ثميناً على أسيك ميموزا الإيفواري بنتيجة 2-1 في العاصمة أبيدجان، مستفيداً من تعادله في مباراة الذهاب بنتيجة 1-1 في مكناس. وبعد انتهاء الشوط الأول بالتعادل السلبي، افتتح الكونغولي كريستوفر إيبايي التسجيل للمغرب الفاسي، قبل أن يتمكن كيفين باكارا من إدراك التعادل لأسيك ميموزا، لتزداد صعوبة المواجهة مع اقتراب نهايتها. وبينما كانت المباراة تتجه إلى ركلات الترجيح، خطف خالد بابا هدف الفوز للمغرب الفاسي في الدقيقة السابعة من الوقت المحتسب بدلاً من الضائع، ليمنح فريقه انتصاراً خارج أرضه بنتيجة 2-1 ويحسم تأهله. وجاء الهدف المتأخر ليضع حداً لمواجهة قوية بين الفريقين، ويمنح النادي المغربي بطاقة العبور بمجموع المباراتين بنتيجة 3-2. ولحق المغرب الفاسي بمواطنه نهضة بركان، وصيف البطولة، الذي ضمن بدوره التأهل بعد إقصاء ستار سبورت أكاديمي السيراليوني، بالفوز عليه ذهاباً وإياباً. ويعزز تأهل الفريقين الحضور المغربي في المرحلة المقبلة من البطولة، بعدما نجحا في تجاوز منافسيهما في الدور التمهيدي الثاني. الهلال السوداني يكرر فوزه على سيداما بونا وفي العاصمة الرواندية كيغالي، التي يتخذها الهلال السوداني ملعباً بيتياً، كرر الفريق فوزه على ضيفه سيداما بونا الإثيوبي بنتيجة 2-0، ليحجز مقعده في مرحلة المجموعات. وكان الهلال قد فاز بالنتيجة نفسها في مباراة الذهاب، ليحسم التأهل بمجموع المباراتين بنتيجة 4-0، مؤكداً تفوقه على منافسه في المواجهتين. وجاءت ثنائية الفريق السوداني في الشوط الأول، إذ افتتح إرنست لوزولو التسجيل في الدقيقة 33، قبل أن يضيف محمد عبد الرحمن «الغربال» الهدف الثاني في الوقت المحتسب بدلاً من الضائع للشوط. ومنح الانتصار الهلال فرصة مواصلة مشواره القاري، كما عوض جماهيره جزئياً عن خروج غريمه التقليدي المريخ من المسابقة، بعدما ودع البطولة السبت على يد حوريا الغيني بركلات الترجيح. وبهذا التأهل، يواصل الهلال تمثيل الكرة السودانية في البطولة، وسط تطلعات إلى تقديم أداء قوي في مرحلة المجموعات والمنافسة على بلوغ الأدوار الإقصائية. سيمبا وكولوم يكملان قائمة المتأهلين وشهدت بقية مباريات الدور التمهيدي الثاني تأهل سيمبا التنزاني، بعدما حقق فوزاً عريضاً على فريق 15 أوغوستو القادم من غينيا الاستوائية بنتيجة 3-0. وجاء الانتصار ليمنح سيمبا تفوقاً كبيراً في مجموع المباراتين بنتيجة 9-1، بعدما كان قد حقق نتيجة إيجابية في لقاء الذهاب، ليعبر إلى المرحلة المقبلة بأفضلية واضحة. كما تأهل كولومب الكاميروني إلى مرحلة المجموعات، عقب فوزه على تينغيت السنغالي بهدف دون رد في مباراة الإياب، مستفيداً من انتصاره في لقاء الذهاب بنتيجة 2-0، ليحسم المواجهة بمجموع 3-0. وتعكس هذه النتائج اتساع رقعة المنافسة بين أندية القارة، مع نجاح فرق من تونس وموريتانيا والمغرب والسودان وتنزانيا والكاميرون في حجز مقاعدها بالمرحلة الرئيسية من البطولة. قرعة المجموعات الأربعاء المقبل تتجه أنظار الأندية المتأهلة إلى قرعة مرحلة المجموعات من دوري أبطال أفريقيا، المقرر إجراؤها الأربعاء المقبل، حيث ستتحدد مواجهات المرحلة المقبلة ومسارات المنافسة نحو الأدوار الإقصائية. وتكتسب القرعة أهمية كبيرة بالنسبة إلى الفرق التي تجاوزت الدور التمهيدي، إذ ستتعرف من خلالها على منافسيها في مجموعاتها، في مرحلة تتطلب الاستعداد لمواجهات أكثر صعوبة أمام أندية تسعى بدورها إلى المنافسة على اللقب القاري. ومع اكتمال تأهل مجموعة من الأندية، تتطلع الفرق إلى استثمار نتائجها الإيجابية في الدور التمهيدي ومواصلة المشوار نحو الأدوار المتقدمة، بينما تبدأ الأندية المتأهلة الاستعداد لمرحلة جديدة من المنافسة على أحد أبرز ألقاب كرة القدم الأفريقية. الأفريقي التونسي مازيمبي دوري أبطال أفريقيا نواذيبو الموريتاني سان بيدرو الإيفواري المغرب الفاسي الهلال السوداني آخر الاخبار انتخابات إسرائيل تهز الأسواق.. بنك أمريكي يتوقع تذبذب الشيكل 3% إغلاق معبر النتيجة الإجمالية. باقي أندية القارة إلى جانب الأندية العربية المتأهلة، اكتملت القائمة بتأهل كل من: 10. سيمبا التنزاني 11. يانغ أفريكانز التنزاني 12. كولومب سبورتيف الكاميروني 13. حوريا كوناكري الغيني على ضيفه «سيداما بونا» الإثيوبي بهدفين دون مقابل، في إياب الدور التمهيدي الثاني على ملعب أماهورو بالعاصمة الرواندية كيغالي، وكان الهلال قد فاز في لقاء الذهاب بالنتيجة ذاتها (2-0)، ليتأهل الفريق عن جدارة واستحقاق. ​تقدم الهلال في الدقيقة (33) من الشوط الأول بتسديدة زاحفة قوية لمدافعه «لوزولو»، الذي استفاد من تمريرة «كرشوم» المحكمة؛ حاول بعدها الفريق الإثيوبي إحراز هدف التعادل وكاد أن يحقق مراده من كرة قوية تكفل قائم الهلال بصدها، وفي الدقيقة الأخيرة للشوط الأول بذل مدافع الهلال «جوباك» مجهوداً جباراً أثمر هدفاً ثانياً عن طريق قائد الفريق محمد عبد الرحمن. ​وانخفض الأداء في الشوط الثاني رغم التغييرات التي أجراها مدربا الفريقين، واستفاد الهلال من خبرات لاعبيه في المحافظة على النتيجة حتى أعلن الحكم نهاية المباراة بفوز الهلال وتأهله لدور المجموعات، التي ستنطلق بعد إجراء القرعة في (28) أكتوبر الجاري. سونا إنضم لقناة النيلين على واتساب Promotion Content أعشاب ونباتات رجيم وأنظمة غذائية لحوم وأسماك 2026/10/25 فيسبوك ‫X لينكدإن واتساب تيلقرام مشاركة عبر البريد طباعة مقالات ذات صلة رياض
